_about: THE SAMPLE PROJECT'S SCREENPLAY — 36 scenes, the pages the rest of
the sample is derived from.
WHY THIS IS ITS OWN FILE. sample.dragon.json is a static import in
hub.js and feature.js, so every byte of it sits in those pages' first
paint whether or not anybody loads the sample. These pages are bigger
than the whole of the rest of that file and are needed only after a
click, so openSampleProject() reaches them with a dynamic import and
they ship as their own chunk. vite.config.js needs the matching
exception and has it: `data` is ONE chunk every page's entry graph
pulls, so the rule that folds src/data/*.json into it would have put a
quarter of a megabyte on twenty first paints. Keep both halves, or the
lazy import means nothing.
WHY THE LENGTH IS NOT ARBITRARY. Each scene is written to the length
the scene model already claims for it — scenes[].eighths in
sample.dragon.json — measured with script.js's own metric
(LINES_PER_PAGE = 55, action 61 columns, dialogue 35), to a tolerance
of 6%. The 18-day schedule, the day out of days, both call sheets and
the budget are all derived from those eighths, so pages that disagreed
with them would make the sample contradict itself about the one number
everything here is built on. Before this file existed the scene list
claimed 105 pages and the script held 2.3.
IT COMES OUT AT 106.5 PAGES AGAINST THE BREAKDOWN'S 105.0, and that is
the right kind of difference rather than a rounding bug to chase.
Twelve of those lines are the sample notice at the top, which is not
part of the film; the rest is the per-scene tolerance landing slightly
long. A script and a 1st AD's eighths differing by about a page is
what actually happens on a production — eighths are measured in
eighths — so the dashboard reading 106.5 beside a breakdown reading
105.0 is the app being truthful about two different measurements, not
two answers to one question. What would be a bug is the hundred-page
gap this file was written to close. If you edit a scene, keep its line
count inside the eighths it is breaking down from, or change both.
THE DIALOGUE IS TANGLISH AND THE REST OF THE PAGE IS NOT, and the
split is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Dialogue is Tamil written
in the Latin alphabet; scene headings, action and transitions are
English. That is the arrangement a Tamil unit shoots from, and the one
this app already defaults to when it drafts a script, for a reason
that is arithmetic rather than editorial: a screenplay page is a
fixed-width Courier grid, 55 lines of it, and the schedule, the sides
and the budget are all derived from that count. Keeping slug lines and
action in English is what keeps the grid fixed-width.
ROMANISED, NEVER TAMIL SCRIPT. Two reasons and the second is the one
that bites. The codebase's convention — glossary.json's, and what the
gate enforces on every key ending `Tanglish` — is Latin, so the text
survives a font with no Tamil coverage. And `--f-script` deliberately
keeps its Tamil face LAST in the stack, because a Tamil family claims
the Latin glyphs too: promote one and a 600px Courier slug line
becomes 534px of proportional sans, and the grid this file is measured
against stops being fixed-width. The gate's own check walks keys
ending `Tanglish` and would never see these elements, so the check
that covers them lives in the harness that built this file.
A word stays English wherever Chennai says it in English — arrear,
semester, practical, hall ticket, register number, file, form,
signature, certificate, notice period, HR. The register is a character
tool rather than an accident: the corporate floor runs on English and
the campus and the house do not, and the protagonist is measurably
more English on that floor than he is anywhere else. The one fixed
spelling is `pathinonnu`, the arrears count, which is the spine of the
film and is the same word in all 36 scenes.
WHAT IT IS. Original writing, for this demo. The scene structure
follows the public account of Dragon (2025, dir. Ashwath Marimuthu),
which is what the whole sample reconstructs; the dialogue, the action
and every piece of paperwork around it are invented. The first two
elements on the page say so, because the Write module is where
somebody will read these and it is the one place the disclaimer has to
be impossible to miss. The two standing rules for any film that
replaces this one hold here too: no real person beside an invented
detail, and no reproduction of anybody's actual screenplay.

elements.text: SAMPLE PAGES. This screenplay was written for this app, as the pages its demo project is broken down from. It is not Ashwath Marimuthu's screenplay for Dragon (2025) and contains none of that film's dialogue — the scene structure follows the public account of the film, and every line, every action paragraph and all of the paperwork attached to it are invented for this sample. Delete the project, or edit any of it, and nothing is lost.

The dialogue is in Tanglish — Tamil in the Latin alphabet — and the slug lines, action and transitions are in English. That is what a Tamil unit actually shoots from, and it is the only arrangement in which the page count stays arithmetic: screenplay pagination is a fixed-width Courier grid, and this app's schedule, sides and budget are all derived from it.
INT. SCHOOL ASSEMBLY HALL, ASHOK NAGAR - DAY (2014)
Ceiling fans on long stems, turning at four different speeds. Under them, rows of folding chairs and a stage with eight staff on it.
A cloth banner behind the stage. PRIZE DAY 2014. The last digit sits lower than the other three.
A hundred and eighty students in white shirts. At the back, sixty parents standing, because the chairs ran out four rows in.
YOUNG RAGAVAN, 17, aisle seat, fifth row. He is not watching the stage.
He has a slip of paper folded into eighths, opened flat on his knee and angled away from the boy behind him.
On it, in his own handwriting: six subjects, six numbers, and a total at the bottom underlined twice.
He checks the total. He does not need to. He has been checking it since February.
At the lectern a teacher reads citations off index cards, flat, one after another, the way a register is read.
Students go up and come down. The applause starts before each name and stops cleanly after it.
Two of the standing parents at the back are his. The father has his hands behind his back. The mother holds a plastic cover with nothing in it.
The father has found the line with his son's name on it in the programme sheet, and keeps his thumb on it.
On stage, a staff member opens a flat box. Inside, a gold medal on a folded ribbon.
The teacher at the lectern turns an index card over and reads both sides of it.
The citation, flat: highest aggregate in the district. Mathematics, physics, chemistry. No rounding, no moderation.
Then the name.
Young Ragavan folds the slip back into eighths and puts it in his shirt pocket before he stands up.
He walks up the aisle. He does not look at the rows. A boy puts a hand out for him to slap and he misses it, because he has not seen it.
Six steps up to the stage. He takes them one at a time.
The medal goes over his head. The ribbon catches on his ear and he straightens it himself.
He shakes four hands in the order he was given in rehearsal, and he gets the order right.
Applause. It runs longer than the ones before it, and he stands inside it without doing anything with his face.
The teacher turns the microphone towards him. This is not in the programme.
Young Ragavan looks at it for a moment.
YOUNG RAGAVAN
Nandri, sir.
He steps back. The teacher moves the microphone closer again, smiling, waiting for the rest of it.
There is no rest of it.
YOUNG RAGAVAN
(to the hall)
Physics-la naalu mark poachu. Question nine.
The hall laughs. He has not made a joke, and he does not know why they are laughing.
He goes down the six steps and back along the aisle to the fifth row.
At the back, the father has taken his hands out from behind his back.
The mother is not watching the stage either. She is looking along the row of parents beside her, one at a time, in case any of them missed it.
Young Ragavan sits. He takes the slip out of his pocket and unfolds it on his knee.
Under his own total he writes the district figure the teacher read out, and draws a line between them.
They are the same number.
He puts the slip away. He does not take the medal off.
The next citation begins. The hall settles. Nobody is looking at him any more, and he does not appear to need them to.
He opens the flat box on his knee, closes it, opens it again.
Two rows behind him, a boy is already asking somebody what the medal is worth.
Young Ragavan does not turn around.
Through the open doors at the back of the hall: white afternoon on a concrete yard, and a watchman folding a chair.
CUT TO:
EXT. RAGAVAN'S HOUSE, VILLIVAKKAM - DAY (2014)
A narrow street. A house with a gate, and a strip of cement in front of it wide enough for two people to stand on.
YOUNG RAGAVAN is on the strip holding a stack of college prospectuses against his chest, because nobody has told him to put it down.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER, fifties, stands in the open gate in a shirt ironed for the occasion. The application forms are in his hand.
RAGAVAN'S MOTHER is half inside the doorway, where she can hear everything and be seen doing nothing.
Twelve neighbours have come out for this. Two of them have brought their own chairs.
A boy on a two-wheeler slows, understands what is happening, and does not stop.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Mudhalla engineering.
He says it to the street, not to his son.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Naalu varusham. Break illa, second attempt illa.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Apparam masters. Veliya. America, Germany, enga seat kedaikkudho anga.
One of the neighbours repeats the word outside to the neighbour standing next to him.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Apparam kalyanam. Veedu kalyanathukku munnadi mudiyanum, kalyanathukku appuram illa.
He turns the forms over so the printed side faces the street.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Moonu vishayam. Indha order-la.
A neighbour asks what the fees are. The father answers a different question, about the college placement record, and the neighbour takes it.
RAGAVAN'S MOTHER
Mottai maadi innum mudiyala.
She says it to nobody in particular. The father does not turn around.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Adhu mudiyum.
RAGAVAN'S MOTHER
Kalyanathukkulla?
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
Kalyanathukkulla.
Young Ragavan moves the prospectus stack from one arm to the other.
YOUNG RAGAVAN
Naan onnu vechukkalama?
The father hands him the forms instead. The medal box sits on the gate pillar, where somebody put it down and left it.
RAGAVAN'S FATHER
(to the street)
Poana vaaram medal vaangiirukkan.
The neighbours already know. They say so, and congratulate him again anyway.
Young Ragavan looks at the forms. Three sheets. His name is filled in on all three already, in his father's handwriting.
The father puts a hand flat on his son's back, not a push but the shape of one, and the boy goes in through the gate.
The neighbours stay. One of them picks up the medal box, opens it, and passes it along.
The box goes down the line, hand to hand, and comes back closed.
CUT TO:
EXT. ENGINEERING COLLEGE - FRONT BLOCK - DAY
The front block: four storeys, a clock on the face of it nine minutes fast, and a hundred and twenty students moving under it.
A college bus swings in and unloads. Two security men work the gate, checking lanyards with the energy of men who have never once found anything.
RAGAVAN, 26, comes through on foot. No lanyard. The walk of a man who is early.
He is not early. He is nineteen days into a semester that started in June.
The first security man puts a hand up.
RAGAVAN
Mozhangaal epdi irukku, anna?
The hand comes down. Ragavan is past the gate while the answer is still being given, and he takes the answer over his shoulder and nods in the right place.
ANBU, the same age, comes out of the shade of the block to meet him, carrying a lab record with a damp cover sheet.
ANBU
Pathinonnu maniku list-a poduvaanga.
RAGAVAN
Enna list?
ANBU
Enna list-nu unakke theriyum.
RAGAVAN
Record sign vaangittiya?
Anbu lets it go, the way you let go of something you have let go of before.
They walk. The front block belongs to Ragavan in a way that it does not belong to anybody who is only passing through it.
A boy stops him for a signature on a tour form. Ragavan signs it, in the box marked staff.
RAGAVAN
Naan countersign pannitennu sollu.
Two girls on the steps want to know whether the symposium is happening. He says it is, and makes a note on the back of his hand, because it is not.
A boy coming down the steps puts money into his shirt pocket without being asked. Another one takes some out of it, also without being asked.
ANBU
Adhu yaaroda?
RAGAVAN
Edhu dhaan yaaroda, da.
Anbu writes something in the back of the lab record. Not for the record. For himself.
The clock on the front block says twenty past nine. Everybody under it subtracts nine minutes without thinking about it.
ANBU
Moonu varushama andha clock keezhadhaan ulla varom.
RAGAVAN
Onbadhukku mela edhavadhu thappa poiruka?
ANBU
Adhu sariyaa irukkardhu kidaiyadhu.
Ragavan has already stopped listening, because a staff member is coming down the steps with a folder under his arm.
He turns, puts himself in the man's path, and is talking before the man has decided whether to stop.
RAGAVAN
Sir. Second batch oda lab list. Ennkitta irukku sir. Rendu maniku office-ku kondu varen.
The staff member nods and goes. Ragavan does not have the lab list, has never seen the lab list, and now has until two o clock.
ANBU
Unkitta list illa.
RAGAVAN
Rendu maniku irukkum.
A third year with a camera wants a photograph. Ragavan steps in, puts an arm round him, and is gone before the second frame.
Under the arch, a notice board. A clerk is unlocking the glass with a key on a length of string.
The glass comes open. The clerk puts up one sheet and smooths it down with the side of his hand.
Students begin to gather. Not many of them, at first.
ANBU
Pathinonnu-nu sonnen.
Ragavan is watching the clerk, and the clerk is looking for the right key to lock up with.
RAGAVAN
Enna avasaram? Week-pooravum anga dhaan irukkum.
ANBU
Week-pooravum anga dhaan irukkum.
He means it a different way. Ragavan takes it the way it was given and not the way it was meant.
Behind them the corridor fills. Somebody says his name, then two people say it, and then it is a sound rather than a name.
He puts a hand up to all of it without looking to see who it was for.
CUT TO:
INT. COLLEGE CORRIDOR - ARREARS BOARD - DAY
A corridor lit by tubes, with a notice board behind glass at the end of it.
Forty students in front of the glass, in the shape a crowd takes when it has formed around one person.
The person is RAGAVAN. His back is to the board and he is reading it over his own shoulder, for the benefit of the room.
Behind the glass: ARREAR SUBJECTS, REGISTERED CANDIDATES. Four columns, two hundred names, a run of subject codes against each one.
Near the bottom, his name, and beside it a run of codes long enough that the clerk has had to carry it onto a second line.
RAGAVAN
(reading, theatrical)
Onnu.
He taps the glass once for each of them.
RAGAVAN
Rendu. Moonu. Naalu dhaan drawing, adhu subject illa da, adhu oru hobby.
The crowd gives him the laugh. He takes it and keeps going.
RAGAVAN
Anju. Aaru. Ezhu. Ezhu-ku poanen.
ANBU
First class-ku mattum poana.
RAGAVAN
Attendance edukkara class adhu dhaan aachu.
Bigger laugh. A boy at the back writes the codes on his wrist, not for Ragavan, for a bet somebody in the hostel is running.
RAGAVAN
Ettu. Onbadhu. Patthu.
He stops on ten with his palm flat on the glass, like a man finishing a speech, and the crowd gives him the end of it.
RAGAVAN
Patthu. Double figures. Indha college-la yaarum naalaam varushathukku munnadi anga poanadhilla.
Applause, in a corridor, for a list of failures. He accepts it with one hand.
Anbu is not in the crowd. He is at the edge of it, close to the glass, reading the second line of codes carried over under the first.
ANBU
Pathinonnu.
Not loud. He does not have to be.
RAGAVAN
Patthu.
ANBU
December practical rendaavadhu line-la irukku. Rendaavadhu line-a yaarum padikkaradhilla.
He puts a finger on the glass under it and leaves the finger there.
The crowd leans in to look. One of them counts under his breath and arrives where Anbu arrived.
RAGAVAN
(to the crowd)
Ivan nalla nyaabagam vechirukkara mosamaana friend.
The laugh comes back, smaller. The crowd begins to come apart into its parts: lectures, canteen, somewhere else.
ANBU
Pathinonnu.
RAGAVAN
Thirupi sollu, pannerandu aagidum.
ANBU
Adhu apdilaam velai seyyadhu.
The last of them go. The corridor empties out to its own length again.
Ragavan stays in front of the glass a second longer than the performance needed.
He looks at the second line. Then he puts his hand over the reflection of his own face and moves off.
CUT TO:
INT. COLLEGE CANTEEN - DAY
Seventy students, four staff, and a ceiling fan moving the smell of oil from one end of the room to the other.
Steel tumblers going down on steel tables. A queue at the counter that is not a queue.
RAGAVAN has the corner table, which is the good table, and he did not get there first.
Two boys stand at the end of it waiting for a verdict on something. ANBU sits across from him with a notebook open.
The notebook is ruled, and it has dates down the left hand side.
RAGAVAN
(to the two boys)
Aalukku ambadhu, rendu maniku yaaru adhula okkaandhirukkaango avangaluku seat. Adhu rule illa, adhu nadakka poradhu adhu dhaan.
They accept it. It is not a good verdict but it was delivered quickly.
He has a tea in front of him that he has not paid for. The counter man brought it over.
ANBU
Rendu mani.
RAGAVAN
Hm.
ANBU
Lab list. Second batch. Adhu unkitta irukkunu oru staff-kitta sonniye.
RAGAVAN
Unkitta pen irukka?
Anbu gives him the pen. Ragavan writes LAB LIST on his hand under the first thing written on his hand, and gives the pen back.
ANBU
Andha kai-la naalu vishayam irukku.
RAGAVAN
Periya kai da.
Anbu turns a page and writes the four things down properly, with the date, because one of them has to.
A boy leans in to ask whether the symposium is happening. Ragavan says yes without turning his head.
ANBU
Adhu nadakkala.
RAGAVAN
Innum nadakkala.
The room is aware of the corner table the way a room is aware of a window.
KEERTHI comes in with a record notebook under her arm, takes a tumbler of water, and sits at the end of their table because it is the only place left.
She does not sit down as a guest. She sits down and starts reading.
RAGAVAN
Nee second batch-la dhaane.
KEERTHI
Aama.
RAGAVAN
Appo unkitta lab list irukkum.
KEERTHI
Oru list-la en per irukku. Adhu veru vishayam.
RAGAVAN
Adhuvum oru aarambam.
She looks up for the first time. He has already turned his hand over so that she cannot read it.
KEERTHI
Second batch list yen unakku venum?
RAGAVAN
Yaarukku edhu yen venum?
KEERTHI
Adhu bathil illa, adhu innum chinna kelvi.
Anbu, without looking up from the notebook, makes a mark in the margin. He has heard this before and he has a mark for it.
RAGAVAN
Onbadhu maniku oruthankitta onnu irukkunu sonnen. Ippo rendu mani.
KEERTHI
Apparam enna?
RAGAVAN
Apparam adhu ennakitta irukkum.
KEERTHI
Illa. Apparam. Ellathukkum apparam.
It is an ordinary question in a canteen. Nothing in the room changes. He answers it the way he answers everything, at speed.
RAGAVAN
Campus placement. Apparam veliyur. Apparam vandhu indha canteen-a vaangi nalla fan vechu tharen.
The nearest four tables laugh. One of them repeats the part about the fan.
Keerthi does not laugh. She is looking at him the way you look at a sum that has come out too easily.
KEERTHI
Ethana arrear?
The table goes quiet, delightedly, the way a room goes quiet when somebody has walked into something.
RAGAVAN
Avan-kitta kelu. Avan vechirukkan.
ANBU
(not looking up)
Pathinonnu.
The canteen takes it like a punchline. Somebody at the far end who cannot have heard the question repeats the number anyway.
Tumblers go up. Eleven is a good number in a canteen at half past one.
Keerthi does not take it as a joke, and does not say that she is not taking it as a joke.
KEERTHI
Ethanaila pathinonnu?
Nobody at the table has that figure. Anbu turns back three pages to look for it.
Keerthi picks up her record notebook and goes to class, which started four minutes ago.
CUT TO:
EXT. ENGINEERING COLLEGE - QUAD - DAY
A quad with a stage end to it: a department banner strung between two pillars, and a mic stand in front of it.
The banner says DEPARTMENT SYMPOSIUM, and under that a date, which is this Friday.
A hundred and fifty students are in the quad, mostly because it is between classes and the quad is where you go.
Nobody is on the stage end. Nobody has been given the job of being on the stage end.
THE CLASSMATE, quiet, a folded jacket over one arm, is working along the edge of the crowd towards the staircase.
RAGAVAN cuts him off without appearing to.
RAGAVAN
Nalla jacket da.
THE CLASSMATE
Adhu en cousin-oda. Kalyanam Sunday anniku.
RAGAVAN
Sunday-ku innum naalu naal irukku.
That is not an argument. It is said as though it were one, and the jacket changes arms.
Black, with something stitched across the whole of the back in gold thread, which neither of them looks at.
THE CLASSMATE
Friday-ku thirupi kudu.
RAGAVAN
Friday.
Ragavan puts it on while walking away, which is the only way he puts anything on.
ANBU watches the handover from the steps and writes a line in the notebook without opening it all the way.
Ragavan arrives at the mic stand. He taps the mic twice. It is live, which surprises everybody including him.
RAGAVAN
Nanbargale. Good afternoon.
A hundred and fifty people turn round for no reason except that somebody has used the microphone.
RAGAVAN
Symposium Friday nadakkudhu. Naan dhaan coordinator.
He is not the coordinator. There is no coordinator. The department is four days away from finding this out.
RAGAVAN
Rendu event, veliyilerundhu oru guest, appuram second half-la ellarukkum tea.
Applause. The tea is the part they applaud.
RAGAVAN
Naalu maniku registration. Ennkitta register pannunga, office-la vendam. Office-la thodachiduvaanga.
A boy shouts a question about whether the guest from outside is confirmed.
RAGAVAN
Edhavadhu confirm aagiruka? Nee confirm-a?
The laugh he gets for that is the biggest of the day, and it buys him the next four days.
He steps back off the mic and turns to come down from the stage end.
The quad sees the back of the jacket for the first time: a dragon in gold thread, head at the shoulder, tail down to the hem.
Somebody at the front says it out loud. Somebody at the back says it louder.
In eight seconds it is a hundred and fifty people saying one word in time, because a quad will do that with any word at all.
Ragavan stops. He does not look confused for longer than it takes him to decide.
Then he turns back, takes the mic off the stand, and gives them the dragon properly: arms out, shoulders square, the whole back of the jacket.
The quad comes apart. Phones go up. A hundred and fifty people are now calling him something that is not his name.
The classmate is at the edge of it on the staircase, watching a jacket that is due at a wedding on Sunday.
THE CLASSMATE
(to nobody)
Friday.
He goes up the stairs. Nobody follows him and nobody asks him anything.
Anbu comes down through the crowd as it breaks up, and the new name reaches him three or four times on the way.
ANBU
Unakku oru per kuduthirukkaanga.
RAGAVAN
Enakku oru Friday kuduthirukkaanga.
ANBU
Adhaiyum kai-la ezhudhikko.
Ragavan looks at his hand. Four things, and the ink has gone in the heat.
RAGAVAN
Innaiku number enna?
ANBU
Nethu enna irundhudho adhe dhaan. Adhu thaana nagaradhu.
Ragavan goes off across the quad in somebody else's jacket, and every second person in it knows him.
Not one of them could say what he is studying.
CUT TO:
INT. DEAN'S OFFICE - DAY
An office with nothing personal in it. A desk, a lamp with a green shade, two chairs, and a cupboard of files that goes up to the ceiling.
A CLERK at a side table stamps a page, turns it, stamps the next one. He does not look up once in the whole scene.
THE DEAN, sixties, is reading a student file. He has been reading it for some time.
RAGAVAN comes in. The jacket is gone. The shirt is tucked in, which is itself a performance.
THE DEAN
(not looking up)
Okkaru.
Ragavan sits. He puts his hands where they can be seen, which he has thought about.
The dean turns the file round and slides one sheet across it. A tour form. A signature in the box marked staff.
THE DEAN
Adhu yaaroda signature?
RAGAVAN
Sir, andha form Thursday varaikkum office-leye kedakkum, pasanga already bus-ukku kaasu kuduthuttaanga.
THE DEAN
Adhu yaaroda signature?
RAGAVAN
Bus dhaan problem. Bus-a naan sari pannitten.
The dean takes the sheet back and puts it in the file, in its place, in order.
THE DEAN
Adhu rendu bathil, rendumay naan ketta bathil illai.
RAGAVAN
Ennudhu, sir.
THE DEAN
Aamaam.
He opens the file near the front and reads off it with no weight on it at all.
THE DEAN
School record. Rendaayirathu padhinaalu. District first, moonu subject, moderation illai.
THE DEAN
Indha vaaram andha varia onbadhu thadava padichirukken.
RAGAVAN
Oru variku onbadhu adhigam, sir.
THE DEAN
Adhukku apparam file chinnadhu.
RAGAVAN
Sir. Placement drive November maasam varudhu.
THE DEAN
Aamaam.
RAGAVAN
Arrear zero irundha dhaan adhula okkaralaam. Apdiyum en per-a serunga.
He says it cleanly. It is the thing he came for, and he has got to it inside four minutes.
THE DEAN
Illai.
RAGAVAN
Ethana-nu neenga kekkave illa.
THE DEAN
Pathinonnu.
He did not have to open the file to get it.
RAGAVAN
Sir, inga varra company arrear sheet padikkaradhilla. Patthu nimisham oru aal kooda okkaandhu pesuvaanga.
THE DEAN
Theriyum. Adhu dhaan en siramam.
THE DEAN
Nee indha room-la anju nimisham irukke. Enakku naalu vilakkam kuduthe, adhula rendai mattum nambinen.
THE DEAN
Adhu entha rendu-nu, solra podhey unakku theriyum.
Ragavan does not answer. It is the first question today that has not had a better question underneath it.
THE DEAN
Naan marukkaradhu un mark-a illai. Mark-a pathi vaadhaadalaam. Mark-ukku oru committee irukku.
THE DEAN
Naan marukkaradhu unnai.
The lamp. The stamp. The cupboard of files going all the way up to the ceiling.
THE DEAN
Andha chair-la okkara ovvoru paiyanum enakku unmai illadha onnai solraan. Sollumbodhey naan nambura oruthan nee mattum dhaan.
RAGAVAN
Adhu apmaanam illa, sir.
THE DEAN
Illai. Adhu dhaan kaaranam.
